phil:shankara: Shankara (also Adi Shankara) was an Indian philosopher of the early eighth century and the most influential systematizer of Advaita Vedanta, the school of non-dualism within Hindu thought. He argued that ultimate reality (Brahman) is a single, undivided consciousness, and that the individual self (atman) is identical with it, so that the apparent multiplicity of the world is a product of ignorance (avidya) and appearance (maya). Through commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras, and through the monastic orders he is traditionally credited with founding, he shaped the course of later Indian philosophy and religious practice.
phil:gandhi: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, called Mahatma, was an Indian political leader and moral thinker whose life spanned 1869 to 1948 and who led the movement for Indian independence from British rule. Drawing on Hindu, Jain, and Christian sources, he developed the practice of satyagraha, or nonviolent resistance grounded in truth-force, together with a commitment to ahimsa (non-harm), simple living, and self-rule (swaraj). His ideas on principled nonviolence and civil disobedience had a lasting influence on later movements for civil rights and social change around the world.
phil:augustine: Augustine of Hippo, who lived from 354 to 430, was a North African bishop and theologian whose writings became foundational for Western Christianity and medieval philosophy. In works such as the Confessions and The City of God he fused Christian doctrine with Neoplatonic thought, exploring memory, time, the will, and the problem of evil, which he understood as a privation of good rather than a substance. His accounts of grace, original sin, and the inward turn toward God shaped centuries of theology and left a deep mark on later reflection on selfhood and human freedom.
phil:boethius: Boethius, who lived roughly from 477 to 524, was a Roman statesman and scholar who sought to preserve and transmit Greek philosophy to the Latin West. He is best known for The Consolation of Philosophy, written while imprisoned awaiting execution, in which the figure of Philosophy consoles him by examining fortune, happiness, providence, and the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human freedom. His translations and commentaries on Aristotle's logic, along with his treatments of universals, made him a crucial bridge between antiquity and medieval Scholasticism.
phil:anselm: Anselm of Canterbury, who lived from 1033 to 1109, was an Italian-born Benedictine monk and Archbishop of Canterbury regarded as a founder of Scholastic theology. He is most famous for the ontological argument set out in his Proslogion, which attempts to prove God's existence from the very concept of God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived. Describing his method as faith seeking understanding, he also advanced influential accounts of the atonement and of the relation between reason and belief.
phil:aquinas: Thomas Aquinas, who lived from 1225 to 1274, was an Italian Dominican friar and the most influential philosopher and theologian of the High Middle Ages. In his vast Summa Theologiae and other works he synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine, arguing that faith and reason are complementary paths to truth and offering his celebrated Five Ways as arguments for God's existence. His treatments of natural law, virtue, and the nature of being became central to Catholic thought and to the enduring tradition known as Thomism.
phil:ockham: William of Ockham, who lived from about 1287 to 1347, was an English Franciscan friar and logician known for his sharp criticism of prevailing metaphysical assumptions. He is associated with the principle of parsimony often called Ockham's razor, which counsels that explanations should not multiply entities beyond necessity, and with nominalism, the view that universals are names rather than real things existing apart from particulars. His work in logic and his defense of a limited role for reason in theology helped push late medieval philosophy toward empiricism and away from earlier realist systems.
phil:maimonides: Maimonides, who lived from 1138 to 1204, was a Jewish philosopher, physician, and legal scholar working in the Islamic world of medieval Spain and Egypt. In his Guide for the Perplexed he sought to reconcile the teachings of the Hebrew Bible with Aristotelian philosophy, developing a rigorously negative theology in which God can be described only by what he is not. His codification of Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah remains authoritative, and his thought influenced later Jewish, Islamic, and Christian philosophers alike.
phil:avicenna: Avicenna, known in Arabic as Ibn Sina and living from 980 to 1037, was a Persian polymath who ranks among the greatest philosophers and physicians of the medieval Islamic world. Building on Aristotle and Neoplatonism, he developed an influential metaphysics centered on the distinction between essence and existence and an argument for a Necessary Being as the ground of all contingent things. His encyclopedic works, especially The Book of Healing and The Canon of Medicine, shaped philosophy and medical teaching in both the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.
phil:averroes: Averroes, known in Arabic as Ibn Rushd and living from 1126 to 1198, was an Andalusian philosopher, jurist, and physician celebrated for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle. He defended the compatibility of philosophy and revelation, arguing that they are two paths to the same truth, and criticized what he saw as the anti-philosophical excesses of earlier thinkers. Through Latin translations his commentaries profoundly influenced medieval European Scholasticism, where he was known simply as the Commentator.
phil:al-ghazali: Al-Ghazali, who lived from about 1058 to 1111, was a Persian theologian, jurist, and mystic whose work reshaped Islamic thought. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers he mounted a searching critique of the Aristotelian rationalism of thinkers like Avicenna, challenging their claims about causation and the eternity of the world, while his later writings integrated Sufi mysticism with orthodox theology. His spiritual autobiography and his synthesis of law, philosophy, and inner experience made him one of the most influential figures in the history of Islam.
phil:descartes: René Descartes, who lived from 1596 to 1650, was a French philosopher and mathematician widely regarded as a founder of modern philosophy. Seeking a secure foundation for knowledge, he adopted a method of radical doubt that led to his famous starting point, cogito ergo sum, and to a sharp dualism between mind and body. His Meditations on First Philosophy and his contributions to analytic geometry made him central to the rise of rationalism and the scientific worldview of the seventeenth century.
phil:spinoza: Baruch Spinoza, who lived from 1632 to 1677, was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent whose rigorous rationalism placed him at the heart of the early Enlightenment. In his Ethics, presented in geometric form, he argued for a single infinite substance identified with God or Nature, of which mind and matter are two aspects, a view often described as pantheism. His challenges to religious orthodoxy, his defense of intellectual freedom, and his analysis of the emotions made him both controversial in his time and deeply influential afterward.
phil:leibniz: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who lived from 1646 to 1716, was a German philosopher and mathematician of extraordinary range, remembered as a leading figure of Continental rationalism. He held that reality is composed of simple, indivisible substances called monads, argued that this is the best of all possible worlds, and formulated principles such as sufficient reason and the identity of indiscernibles. Independently of Newton he developed the calculus, and his work touched on logic, metaphysics, and the reconciliation of divine goodness with the existence of evil.
phil:pascal: Blaise Pascal, who lived from 1623 to 1662, was a French mathematician, physicist, and religious thinker whose reflections combined scientific brilliance with intense spiritual concern. He is remembered in philosophy for the wager that bears his name, which frames belief in God as a prudent bet given the possible stakes, and for the fragmentary Pensées, in which he explored the misery and greatness of the human condition. Aligned with the austere Jansenist movement, he stressed the limits of reason and the role of the heart in grasping ultimate truths.
